first_impression.reaction: Typed 'greek orthodox wedding' on the train because my partner's family is Orthodox and I have no idea what happens. The first lines tell me straight away: it's a sacrament, two parts, no vows. That's already more than I knew. Takeaways are short and real. I'd read them, jump to the step-by-step ceremony and the FAQ, then bookmark it.

journey.quote: A Greek Orthodox wedding is a sacrament, not a ceremony you write yourselves.
journey.reaction: Direct answer in the first line. Good, no fluffy intro about love and islands.
Wait, really? That's the one fact I'll tell my partner tonight. Short and surprising.

journey.quote: Some dates and seasons are closed to weddings, including the weeks before Christmas, Great Lent until Easter Sunday and the first half of August.
journey.reaction: First half of August is closed? That's peak summer in Greece. Specific and useful before anyone picks a date.

journey.quote: Church paperwork and civil paperwork are two separate tracks, and a wedding in Greece adds the local Metropolis, the municipality and the Australian Embassy in Athens.
journey.reaction: Australian Embassy in a quick bullet. I'm in Singapore, so I'm guessing my version of this is different. Fine, but it tells me the page isn't really written for me.

journey.section: Who can marry in the Greek Orthodox Church?
journey.quote: These are the rules for a Greek Orthodox wedding in Australia.
journey.reaction: Hang on, so do these rules apply to me or not? It says the local Metropolis sets them in Greece, but nothing about anywhere else. I'll assume they're roughly similar, but I'm not sure.

journey.section: If one partner is not Orthodox
journey.quote: A baptism performed by a female pastor or member of clergy is not accepted.
journey.reaction: That's exactly the kind of thing nobody would tell you until it's too late. My partner's side would need to know this early. Screenshot.

journey.section: What are the requirements to get married in a Greek Orthodox church?
journey.quote: Once the priest has confirmed that the Church can marry you, the requirements come down to papers, timing, a sponsor and a date the Church allows.
journey.reaction: Four things. Easy to remember. The headings under it match those four, so I can jump.

journey.section: The Service of Betrothal and the rings
journey.quote: There is no moment when you slip a ring onto each other's hand. Tell your photographer, so they are watching the sponsor's hands and not waiting for the couple.
journey.reaction: Love this. A practical tip I'd never think of. The step-by-step section is the bit I actually came for and it's easy to scan.

journey.section: What are stefana, the Orthodox wedding crowns?
journey.reaction: Clear. Short. Answers the question in the heading.

journey.section: How long is a Greek Orthodox wedding?
journey.quote: The length depends on the parish, the priest and how much of the service is sung, so ask your priest for your church's running time.
journey.reaction: Just tell me roughly how long. The heading asks my exact question, then the answer is 'ask your priest'. Is it 30 minutes or two hours? My guests will want to know.

journey.section: Questions to ask the priest and the venue
journey.quote: Ask your priest about your partner's denomination.
journey.reaction: By the FAQ I've read 'ask your priest' a lot of times. I get it, the priest decides. After a while it starts to feel like the page is handing me back my own question.

journey.quote: Its document steps run in a fixed order: each document except passports needs its own Apostille, then a Greek translation; copies go for approval at least four weeks before the date, approval for the Orthodox wedding coming from the Metropolis; and all documents must be issued within three months of the wedding date.
journey.reaction: One giant sentence with semicolons on a phone screen. It says 'fixed order' but it isn't a list, so I lost the order halfway through.

journey.quote: The rite takes place in church, before the Holy Altar.
journey.reaction: Answers the 'can we do it on the beach' question I had in my head. Straight no, plus a pointer to resort chapels. Good FAQ.

journey.section: Questions to ask the priest and the venue
journey.quote: Your Wedded Advisor is a single point of contact who plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments around the service your priest confirms, works in your time zone and quotes in AUD, with the fee agreed in writing before any work begins
journey.reaction: AUD again. So this is an Australian service. Not sure they'd take me on from Singapore.

unanswered_questions: Roughly how long does the service usually run? Even a typical range would do.
Do the eligibility rules and closed dates differ if we marry outside Australia and Greece, for example in Singapore?
What if neither of us has a parish priest yet? How do we find one?
Do you work with couples who aren't Australian?

turn_offs_found.quote: The length depends on the parish, the priest and how much of the service is sung, so ask your priest for your church's running time.
turn_offs_found.why: The heading matches my question word for word, which made me tap it, and then there's no number at all. On a 'how long' question that feels like a dodge, even if the reason is fair.

turn_offs_found.quote: Its document steps run in a fixed order: each document except passports needs its own Apostille, then a Greek translation; copies go for approval at least four weeks before the date, approval for the Orthodox wedding coming from the Metropolis; and all documents must be issued within three months of the wedding date.
turn_offs_found.why: It's a step-by-step process written as one long sentence. On a phone I can't follow the order, and the rest of the page uses lists for exactly this kind of thing.

turn_offs_found.quote: These are the rules for a Greek Orthodox wedding in Australia.
turn_offs_found.why: The heading 'Who can marry in the Greek Orthodox Church?' reads like a general answer, then this line limits it to Australia. Anyone searching from somewhere else is left guessing whether it applies to them.

would_share_with: My partner, for the no-vows line and the step-by-step ceremony
My partner's mum, for the koumbaros rule about not becoming godparent later
A friend with a mixed-faith engagement, for the 'If one partner is not Orthodox' section

cta_reaction.why: I came to understand the ceremony, not to book anything, and the page itself tells me to see a priest first. The links sit in the text with no pop-ups, so they didn't bother me, but 'quotes in AUD' makes me think I'm not the customer. I'd bookmark it.

top_3_changes: Under 'How long is a Greek Orthodox wedding?', give a typical running-time range if a source supports one; if not, say plainly in the first sentence that there is no fixed length, so the heading doesn't promise a number it can't deliver.

Turn the Elounda document steps in 'The church and the paperwork' into a short numbered list (apostille, Greek translation, approval four weeks ahead, issued within three months) so the 'fixed order' is readable on a phone.

Next to 'These are the rules for a Greek Orthodox wedding in Australia.', add one line for couples marrying elsewhere (the local diocese sets the rules, so confirm with it), so non-Australian readers know where they stand.
